title: The Empty Classrooms of ‘American Hagwon’
gist: Nina Li Coomes reviews Min Jin Lee's novel American Hagwon, praising its sociological detail on Korean cram schools but arguing its characters become flat vehicles for a message and that it ignores how the 'model minority' education narrative has been used against other minorities after the 2023 affirmative-action ruling.

insights.claim: As of 2022, 78.3 percent of South Korean elementary-aged students attended private hagwons, for-profit cram schools, which in the United States are less prevalent and often attached to Korean American churches.
insights.speaker: Nina Li Coomes
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of South Korea's private tutoring economy, a durable consumer-services sector.
insights.locator: These are not trivial after-school activities

insights.claim: American Hagwon (656 pages, September 2026) follows the Koh family from 1992 to 2007 across South Korea, Australia and the United States, with the 1997 Asian financial crisis among the shocks driving their reliance on education as the route to stability.
insights.speaker: Nina Li Coomes
insights.so_what: Illustrates how macro shocks reinforce immigrant households' education-focused strategies.

insights.claim: The reviewer's own experience was that white classmates were seen as gifted through effort or talent while her academic performance was attributed to her ethnicity, illustrating the essentialization of Asians and academic achievement.
insights.speaker: Nina Li Coomes
insights.so_what: Stereotypes of Asian academic excellence have shaped US educational policy debates.
insights.locator: One of the first places I was made aware of my race

insights.claim: The reviewer argues the novel is richly researched in its settings and Korean American community politics but sacrifices character complexity for social commentary, especially in the second half of its nearly 700 pages.
insights.speaker: Nina Li Coomes
insights.so_what: Quality judgment on a major fall 2026 literary release.
insights.quote: its characters start to flag under the weight of those questions

insights.claim: Villain Danbi is a one-dimensional 'emblem of an unmeaningful life' while Mido is 'relentlessly, tediously good', and the reviewer argues the ultimate antagonist should have been societal, such as inequality, poverty or lack of access to higher education.
insights.speaker: Nina Li Coomes
insights.locator: Take Danbi, the book’s consummate villain.

insights.claim: The novel is ambivalent on its moral, curious about education as a route up for immigrant parents but questioning whether heavy schooling benefits South Korean children even as its heroes succeed teaching in cram schools.
insights.speaker: Nina Li Coomes
insights.so_what: Mirrors unresolved policy debate about South Korea's education intensity.
insights.locator: What, then, is the moral that Lee is so intent on promoting?

themes.theme: Affirmative action and the education narrative

insights.claim: After the 2023 Supreme Court ruling striking down affirmative action in a case led by Asian American students and backed by conservative activists, data show little to no change in Asian American enrollment rates at Ivy League institutions.
insights.speaker: Nina Li Coomes
insights.so_what: Shows that race-blind admissions did not deliver the promised gains to Asian American applicants.

insights.claim: The reviewer argues that the Asian American pursuit of education has been used as a cudgel to dismantle education access for other minorities, a dynamic that the novel ignores, so its framing of Asian education as innocent is outdated.
insights.speaker: Nina Li Coomes
insights.so_what: Political contestation over education and race will continue to shape admissions policy and litigation.
insights.quote: The rules of engagement have changed, and this novel doesn’t seem to have noticed.
insights.locator: Which is all to say, though American Hagwon tries
